Structural Variant detection¶

INRAe-IFB-INSERM Bioinformatics School 2026

  • Gabrièle Adam - INRAE

Definition¶

Structural variations (SV) are genomic rearrangements with a size superior to 50pbs. They can change copy number, orientation and/or location of a sequence. They can be:

  • Unbalanced (change DNA content):
    • Deletion
    • Duplication
    • Insertion
  • Balanced (preserve DNA content):
    • Inversion
    • Translocation

Different type of SVs¶

Figures from Alkan C, Coe BP, Eichler EE. Genome structural variation discovery and genotyping. Nat Rev Genet. 2011 May;12(5):363-76. doi: 10.1038/nrg2958

Deletion: Loss of a segment of DNA¶

Duplication: Additional copy of a segment¶

Tandem duplication: the copy sit right next to the original¶

Interspeed duplication: the copy is inserted elsewhere in the genome, on te same chromosome or not¶

Insertion¶

Novel insertion: A new sequence that is not in the reference is added¶

Mobile element insertion: a transposable element has inserted a new copy¶

Inversion: A segment is cut out, flipped 180°, and reinserted in place. No DNA is gained or lost¶

Translocation: A segment moves to a different location, usually to another chromosome. We can talk about reciprocal translation when 2 chromosomes swap pieces.¶

How can we detect structural variation in an alignment?¶

There are 5 methods to detect a SV in the alignment, what do think they are? Hints: How will a SV impact the alignment?

All method infer SVs from how sequencing data deviate from the reference. These deviations show up in coverage, read-pair geometry, read alignment, or sequence and assembly comparison. No single method captures all SV classes, so methods differ mainly in which types and size ranges they can resolve.

Read depth¶

The coverage is proportional to the copy number. Best for DEL, DUP, CNV. Blind to balanced events (INV, reciprocal translocation) and to insertions. Breakpoints are only approximate (window resolution).

Paired-Reads (discordant pairs)¶

Paired reads should map with the expected orientation and insert size. Deviations reveal the SV type:

  • larger insert = DEL
  • smaller insert = INS
  • same orientation of the reads = INV
  • mates on different chromosomes = BND Breakpoints are only approximate. Insertions longer than the insert size are poorly sized. Unreliable when mates fall in repeats.

Split reads¶

A single read spans a breakpoint, so its alignment is split (supplementary or soft-clipped, cf Mapping course). This gives base-pair resolution of the junction. Requires the read to cross the junction, which works poorly with short reads at repeat boundaries. Cannot easily resolve insertions longer than read length.

De novo-assembly¶

Reads around candidate breakpoints are reassembled to reconstruct the alternative allele sequence. De novo (ideally haplotype-resolved) assemblies are aligned to the reference or to each other, and rearrangements are called from synteny breaks.

Short reads or long reads ?¶

Short reads (Illumina): Depending on the tool and data quality

  • low recall: 10–70% of SVs detected
  • low precision: up to 90% false positives
  • difficulty characterizing complex SVs (imprecise alignment in repetitive regions and low resolution)
Consensus calling with several detection tools can be useful with short-read data.

Long reads (PacBio/MinION):

  • better characterization of alterations in repetitive regions
  • low coverage depth is sufficient (15–30x)

Criteria¶

  • Do I have long or short reads?
  • How many samples do I have?
  • What type of SVs I am looking for ?
  • Is my depth of coverage enough?
  • Which should be proiritize? Specificity or sensibility ?
  • What is the output of the tool ?

Where are we in the workflow ?¶

Mapping¶

Short Reads bowtie2 --threads 4 --very-sensitive --no-unal -x genomeRef -1 R1.fq.gz -2 R2. fq.gz -S output.sam

Long Reads minimap2 -t 4 -ayYL --MD --eqx -x asm20 Ref.fa subreads > output.sam

  • a output in sam format
  • -Y use soft clipping for supplementary alignments
  • -L write CIGAR with >65535 ops at the CG tag
  • -MD output the MD tag
  • --eqx write =/X CIGAR operator
  • asm20Use this if the average divergence is around several percent.

Practice¶

Project:¶

Zymoseptoria tritici: an ascomycete fungus, a pathogen of bread wheat, causing a foliar disease (Septoria tritici blotch, STB).

  • Main disease of wheat (up to 50% yield loss).
  • Haploid; 40 Mb genome sequenced in 2011: 13 core chromosomes + 8 accessory chromosomes.
  • Strain sequenced with two technologies: Illumina and MinION.

Purpose: Sequencing is used to analyse isolates, mock communities and field samples to determine the pathogen population composition related to azole resistance

Data and Tools¶

Data: a Zymoseptoria tritici strain sequenced with both Illumina and MinION. → each read set was aligned to the reference genome with the dedicated tools → the data were subset to the first 500 kb of chr10

Tools:

  • Delly (Bioinformatics, Volume 28, Issue 18, 15 September 2012, Pages i333–i339, https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/bts378)
  • Sniffles (Nature Methods, volume 15, pages 461–468 (2018), https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-018-0001-7) with NGMLR mapping

Where are we and in which folder are we going to work ?¶

Where are we ?

In [ ]:
pwd

How are we going to the right folder ?

In [ ]:
cd pathway_to/atelier_variant/TP_structural_variants

1.SV detection from Illumina short-read data¶

First, we will use Delly (paper here: doi: 10.1093/bioinformatics/bts378, code there: https://github.com/dellytools/delly). We start by working on short-read data.

In [ ]:
module load delly/0.8.3

How do you find out which command to use to run Delly?

In [ ]:
delly | cat

And more specifically, how do you run Delly for variant calling?

In [ ]:
delly call | cat

1.1 Indexing¶

As seen in the previous lectures, we will start by indexing our alignment and our reference. Load samtools and index the reference and the alignment:

In [ ]:
module load samtools/1.13
In [ ]:
samtools faidx Zymoseptoria_tritici.fa
In [ ]:
samtools index mapping_illumina_chr10_500kb.bam

1.2 Variant calling¶

Now, let's use Delly for variant calling:

In [ ]:
delly call -g Zymoseptoria_tritici.fa  -o SV_calling_illumina.bcf  mapping_illumina_chr10_500kb.bam

To look at this result:

In [ ]:
head SV_calling_illumina.bcf

Here the format is not VCF but BCF, so it needs to be converted.

In [ ]:
# Convert to VCF
module load bcftools/1.10.2
bcftools view SV_calling_illumina.bcf > SV_calling_illumina.vcf

Now we can look at our variants

Step 1: look at the file header only:

In [ ]:
grep "^#" SV_calling_illumina.vcf

Step 2: look at the first 3 variants only:

In [ ]:
grep -v "^#" SV_calling_illumina.vcf | head -n3

1.3 Counting SVs¶

How many variants are in the file?

In [ ]:
# How many variants?
grep -v -c "^#" SV_calling_illumina.vcf
In [ ]:
# How many good-quality variants?
grep -v "^#" SV_calling_illumina.vcf | grep -v -c "LowQual"
In [ ]:
# How many variants are of good quality in each type (DEL,DUP, INS, BND, etc ...?
grep -v "^#" SV_calling_illumina.vcf | grep -v "LowQual" | grep -c "<DEL>"

1.3 Extracting deletion information in a separate file¶

Extract good-quality deletions:

In [ ]:
grep -v "^#" SV_calling_illumina.vcf | grep -v "LowQual" | grep "<DEL>"
In [ ]:
# Retrieve variant start positions
grep -v "^#" SV_calling_illumina.vcf | grep -v "LowQual" | grep "<DEL>" | \
cut -f1,2 > delly_del_start.txt
💡 Sed Command

sed (stream editor) reads a file line by line and replaces text, like "Find & Replace" in Word, but on the command line.

The syntax is always:

sed "s/WHAT_TO_FIND/WHAT_TO_PUT_INSTEAD/g"
Part Meaning
s substitute (replace)
/ separator between the parts
g global: replace every occurrence on the line, not only the first
💡 Tip: why the \ at the end of the line?

This command is long, so it is split over two lines to make it easier to read.

But for the terminal, pressing Enter means "run the command now". The backslash \ at the end of a line tells the terminal: "wait, the command is not finished, it continues on the next line".

So these two versions are exactly the same command:

grep -v "^#" file.vcf | grep "<DEL>" | cut -f8

grep -v "^#" file.vcf | grep "<DEL>" | \
cut -f8

⚠️ The \ must be the very last character of the line: even an invisible space after it breaks the command.

In [ ]:
# Retrieve the other information
grep -v "^#" SV_calling_illumina.vcf | grep -v "LowQual" | grep "<DEL>" | \
cut -f8 | cut -d ";" -f1,4,5,13 | sed "s/;/\t/g" > delly_del_info.txt

Merge the 2 files and format:

In [ ]:
# Merge the two files
paste -d '\t' delly_del_start.txt delly_del_info.txt > delly_del.txt
In [ ]:
# Format and clean up
awk '{OFS="\t" ; print $1,$2,$4,$3,$5,$6}' delly_del.txt | sed "s/END=//g" > delly_del.tsv
💡 Tip: what does awk do here?

awk is a tool that reads a file line by line and sees each line as a row of columns, like a spreadsheet. Each column gets a name: $1 is the 1st column, $2 the 2nd, $3 the 3rd, and so on.

Here we use it to reorder the columns, so that the start and end of each deletion sit next to each other.

The command, piece by piece:

Piece Meaning
'{ ... }' the instructions to apply to every line
OFS="\t" separate the output columns with a tab (Output Field Separator)
print $1,$2,$4,$3,$5,$6 write the columns in this new order (note that $4 now comes before $3)
delly_del.txt the file to read

Clean up:

In [ ]:
rm delly_del_info.txt delly_del_start.txt delly_del.txt

2. SV detection from MinION long-read data¶

For long-read data, we will use another caller: Sniffles (paper here: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-018-0001-7, code there: https://github.com/fritzsedlazeck/Sniffles)

In [ ]:
module load sniffles/1.0.11
In [ ]:
sniffles --help

No reference genome needed!

2.1 Indexing the alignment¶

In [ ]:
samtools index mapping_minion_chr10_500kb.bam

2.2 Variant calling¶

In [ ]:
sniffles -l 100 -m mapping_minion_chr10_500kb.bam -v SV_calling_minion.vcf
In [ ]:
grep '^#' SV_calling_minion.vcf

2.3 Counting SVs¶

How many SVs are located on chr10?

In [ ]:
cat SV_calling_minion.vcf | grep ^chr_10 | wc -l

How many are deletions/duplications/translocations/invertions/...?

In [ ]:
cat SV_calling_minion.vcf | grep ^chr_10 | grep "DEL" | wc -l

2.4 Extracting deletion positions in a separate file¶

Extract the chromosome and start position of each deletion

In [ ]:
cat SV_calling_minion.vcf | grep ^chr_10 | grep "DEL" | cut -f -1,2 > sniffles_del_start.txt
In [ ]:
Extract the end position of each deletion
In [ ]:
cat SV_calling_minion.vcf | grep ^chr_10 | grep "DEL" | cut -d ";" -f 4 | cut -d "=" -f 2 > sniffles_del_stop.txt

Extract additional deletion information

In [ ]:
cat SV_calling_minion.vcf | grep ^chr_10 | grep "DEL" | cut -f 8 | cut -d ";" -f 1 > sniffles_del_infos.txt

Paste everything together

In [ ]:
paste sniffles_del_start.txt sniffles_del_stop.txt sniffles_del_infos.txt > sniffles_del.tsv

Now clean-up

In [ ]:
rm sniffles_del_start.txt sniffles_del_stop.txt sniffles_del_infos.txt

3.Compare Delly and Sniffles results¶

Here we will look at the Delly and Sniffles results

In [ ]:
cat delly_del.tsv
In [ ]:
cat sniffles_del.tsv

Are the deletions at the same positions?

Conclusion¶

SV detection lacks precision and produces both false positives and false negatives.

  • Need to cross-check results across different tools and technologies
  • Need to make proper use of each tool's quality metrics
  • Need sufficient sequencing depth (especially for heterozygous variants)

Visually checking the results in IGV increases confidence in the detected SVs.
